title: Transformer Decoder — 7 Learning Questions
subtitle: Topic: Autoregressive Text Generation and Decoder Architecture · Subject: Transformers and LLM Architecture. Seven preserved questions, four length-balanced choices each, seven illustrated learning scenes, and beginner-first explanations.

TRANSFORMER DECODER · VISUAL STUDY MAP

Read the existing tokens. Predict one more. Repeat.

The diagram shows a possible continuation, not a guaranteed one. During inference, the model repeatedly chooses and appends one token.

questions.stem: What is a Transformer Decoder, and how does it enable Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT to generate text one token at a time by predicting what should come next?
options: A decoder generates every word of a paragraph simultaneously, then sorts them into a sentence afterward, without conditioning each word on earlier output tokens.
A decoder copies an entire sentence from its training examples and changes only punctuation, instead of computing a new probability distribution for each token.
A Transformer Decoder predicts the next token from earlier tokens and generates text by repeatedly extending the sequence. Decoder-only models such as GPT use causal self-attention for this process.
A decoder requires a separate encoder to choose each next token, so decoder-only systems cannot generate words without an additional external network.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A Transformer Decoder predicts the next token from earlier tokens and generates text by repeatedly extending the sequence. Decoder-only models such as GPT use causal self-attention for this process. Imagine a language model writing a new scene for a radio drama. It reads the opening line, predicts one possible next token, and appends it. The longer passage becomes context for the next prediction. This is how a Transformer Decoder generates text step by step. It does not create every sentence at once or search for an exact stored script.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: A decoder-only Transformer maps a sequence of input token IDs to hidden states, then predicts a probability distribution for the token following each context position. At generation time, it starts with prompt tokens, computes next-token logits from the final position, selects a token, appends that token, and repeats until a stop condition or length limit. The model usually computes many positions in parallel during teacher-forced training, but at inference each newly committed token depends on previously committed output. Tokens are vocabulary units, not necessarily full words.

01 · What decoder means

Each newly generated token becomes context for the next prediction

GPT-style decoder-only models output a probability distribution over possible next tokens and then select one token to continue.

questions.stem: Why does a Transformer Decoder use Causal Masking (Masked Self-Attention), and how does preventing a token from seeing future tokens allow the model to learn to generate text in the correct order?
options: Causal masking prevents each training position from accessing later tokens. This keeps next-token predictions dependent only on available earlier context, matching the information the model has during text generation.
Causal masking hides all earlier words, forcing each position to use future tokens and preventing the decoder from learning left-to-right relationships.
Causal masking deletes low-probability vocabulary words after Softmax, making output deterministic rather than controlling which input positions can be attended to.
Causal masking prevents the decoder from seeing any input tokens during training, leaving it unable to learn relationships from the sequence.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Causal masking prevents each training position from accessing later tokens. This keeps next-token predictions dependent only on available earlier context, matching the information the model has during text generation. Picture writing instructions for planting a garden, one word at a time. When predicting the third word, you should not secretly read the seventh word. A causal mask enforces that rule inside decoder self-attention: each position can use current and earlier tokens, but not later positions. During training, many positions can be processed together while the mask blocks future information. During generation, the model follows the same left-to-right information rule.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: In masked self-attention, a Query at position i may see Keys and Values at positions j≤i; positions j>i are masked before Softmax, commonly by setting their attention logits to negative infinity. This produces a triangular attention matrix. During training the model can process a full target sequence at once, using shifted labels and a causal mask to prevent answers leaking from future target positions. During autoregressive inference there are no future generated tokens yet, but maintaining a causal structure stays consistent with training.
questions.figure:
02 · Causal masking

Future positions are blocked during decoder self-attention

The diagonal stays visible because a position may attend to itself. During training, causal masking prevents leakage from later target tokens.

questions.stem: When a Transformer Decoder receives the input "The sun rises in the," how does it process the existing tokens, predict a likely next token such as "east," and repeatedly use newly generated tokens to continue producing a sentence?
options: The decoder generates an entire finished sentence at once, then looks backward to determine which token should have appeared directly after the original prompt.
The decoder always copies the exact continuation stored for this phrase, regardless of different instructions or earlier context that might change the output.
The decoder must first translate the prompt into encoder states and produce a complete answer, without ever adding its own predicted tokens as context.

The decoder represents the provided tokens, predicts probabilities for the next token, selects one, and appends it to the context. It repeats this process until a stop condition or output limit is reached.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The decoder represents the provided tokens, predicts probabilities for the next token, selects one, and appends it to the context. It repeats this process until a stop condition or output limit is reached. Start with “The sun rises in the.” A decoder calculates probabilities for possible next tokens; “east” might receive a high score. After selecting that token, the text becomes “The sun rises in the east.” The decoder then predicts again using the expanded context. It may add punctuation, more words, or a special end token. This repeated process is called autoregressive generation .
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: Tokenize the prompt “The sun rises in the”. The decoder uses embeddings plus positional information and repeated causally masked Transformer blocks to form contextual hidden states. A final projection gives vocabulary logits for the next position; after Softmax and a chosen decoding strategy, a token such as “east” may be selected. The new token is appended to the context, so the next inference step predicts from “The sun rises in the east”. The actual token is not guaranteed to be “east”: it depends on the model, tokenization and sampling method. KV caching can avoid recomputing earlier Key and Value projections for the extension.

questions.stem: What happens inside a decoder-only Transformer block, from token embeddings and positional information to Masked Multi-Head Self-Attention, Residual Connections, Layer Normalization, and Feed-Forward Networks, and how does stacking multiple decoder blocks produce contextual representations?
options: Token embeddings go directly to the output vocabulary layer without attention or feed-forward processing, so later blocks cannot refine the token representations.

A decoder-only block processes token embeddings and positional information through causally masked multi-head attention, residual connections, normalization, and feed-forward layers. Repeated blocks build contextual hidden representations without using future tokens.
Each decoder block independently selects final vocabulary words, then passes those finished words to the next block instead of contextual hidden representations.
Causal attention operates only during generation, while residual connections and normalization run only during training, so the model uses different layer structures.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A decoder-only block processes token embeddings and positional information through causally masked multi-head attention, residual connections, normalization, and feed-forward layers. Repeated blocks build contextual hidden representations without using future tokens. Imagine a text assistant reading a long announcement from an airport. Its tokens first become numerical embeddings with position information. Inside each decoder block, masked multi-head self-attention connects each position with available earlier context. Feed-forward layers transform the resulting features, while residual connections and LayerNorm help information and gradients flow. Stacking blocks builds richer representations.
questions.technicalExplanation:
Detailed explanation: Decoder-only Transformers receive token embeddings with position information. Each repeated block generally contains causal multi-head self-attention, an FFN, layer normalization (or a similar norm), and two residual connections. A widely used Pre-LN pattern is x ← x + Attention(Norm(x)), then x ← x + FFN(Norm(x)). The output hidden states become increasingly contextual. The original Transformer used a Post-LN architecture instead. This tested PyTorch snippet implements a single Pre-LN causal block without the embedding or vocabulary head:
import torch
from torch import nn

class TinyDecoderBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=16, heads=4):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(d, heads, batch_first=True)
        self.norm2 = nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.ffn = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(d, 4*d), nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4*d, d)
        )

    def forward(self, x):
        t = x.size(1)
        # True in nn.MultiheadAttention means "block this position".
        mask = torch.triu(
            torch.ones(t, t, dtype=torch.bool, device=x.device), 1
        )
        h = self.norm1(x)
        a, _ = self.attn(h, h, h, attn_mask=mask, need_weights=False)
        x = x + a
        return x + self.ffn(self.norm2(x))

torch.manual_seed(4)
x = torch.randn(2, 5, 16)
y = TinyDecoderBlock()(x)
print(tuple(y.shape))       # (2, 5, 16)
print(torch.isfinite(y).all().item())  # True
Use True entries in the nn.MultiheadAttention boolean attention mask to block future tokens; this convention differs from certain lower-level attention APIs.

questions.stem: How does a Transformer Decoder convert its final hidden states into next-token predictions using output projection, logits, Softmax probabilities, and decoding strategies such as Greedy Decoding, Temperature Sampling, Top-k Sampling, and Top-p Sampling?
options: Logits are already valid probabilities, so temperature and Top-k simply sort the vocabulary without changing how the model chooses among candidate tokens.
Greedy decoding picks a random candidate, while Top-k excludes the highest-scoring group; both claims reverse how common decoding strategies work.

The decoder projects its final hidden state into vocabulary logits, and Softmax converts them into probabilities. Greedy decoding picks the highest score, while temperature, top-k, and top-p sampling control randomness and candidate selection.
Top-p always keeps exactly p vocabulary items, while increasing temperature always improves accuracy, regardless of the model's scores or task.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The decoder projects its final hidden state into vocabulary logits, and Softmax converts them into probabilities. Greedy decoding picks the highest score, while temperature, top-k, and top-p sampling control randomness and candidate selection. Suppose a writing assistant has four plausible words to finish a sentence. Its final layer produces raw scores called logits . Softmax converts them into probabilities. Greedy decoding chooses the highest-scoring token; temperature changes how concentrated the choices are. Top-k samples among a fixed number of leading candidates, while Top-p samples within a probability-mass cutoff.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: The final hidden state h at the last position is mapped to vocabulary logits z=hW_vocab+b (or a tied embedding projection). After optional temperature scaling and token filters, probabilities are p=Softmax(z/T). Greedy decoding takes argmax each time. Temperature below 1 sharpens the distribution; above 1 flattens it. Top-k restricts sampling to the k highest-probability tokens. Top-p (nucleus) uses the smallest ranked set whose cumulative probability reaches at least p. The remaining probabilities are renormalized before sampling. With illustrative probabilities east .58, west .23, sky .12, dawn .07: top-k=2 keeps east/west, while top-p=.9 keeps east/west/sky. Sampling introduces variation; neither top-k nor top-p guarantees better factuality.
questions.figure:
05 · From logits to words

Output logits become probabilities; decoding rules select the next token

Percentages are illustrative. Top-k keeps a fixed number; top-p keeps the smallest high-probability set reaching a threshold.

questions.stem: How does the architecture of a decoder-only Transformer differ from the decoder in the original Encoder-Decoder Transformer, particularly regarding Cross-Attention, encoder outputs, causal masking, and information flow, and why are decoder-only architectures widely used for autoregressive language generation?
options: Decoder-only models rely on causal self-attention over a single sequence. The original Transformer decoder also includes cross-attention to separate encoder outputs, allowing generation conditioned on a processed source sequence.
Decoder-only models require encoder cross-attention to generate each word, while original encoder-decoders never use causal masks for any output token.
Decoder-only Transformers can see their own future output tokens, while encoder-decoder Transformers cannot access source text during generation.
Decoder-only and encoder-decoder architectures have identical attention blocks, and their only structural difference is the tokenizer chosen for each model.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Decoder-only models rely on causal self-attention over a single sequence. The original Transformer decoder also includes cross-attention to separate encoder outputs, allowing generation conditioned on a processed source sequence. Picture two translation tools. A GPT-style decoder-only model places instructions and prior text in one token stream, then generates using causal self-attention. The original Transformer encoder-decoder structure first builds source representations with an encoder. Its decoder uses causal self-attention for the growing output and cross-attention to access the source. Both can generate one token at a time, but their ways of reading source information differ.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: The original 2017 encoder–decoder Transformer has an encoder that processes source tokens using bidirectional self-attention. Its decoder has masked self-attention over earlier target tokens plus a cross-attention sublayer whose Queries come from decoder states and whose Keys/Values come from encoder outputs. The original used residual connections and Post-LayerNorm around its sublayers. A GPT-style decoder-only Transformer has no separate encoder or encoder–decoder cross-attention; it handles prompt and generated tokens in one causally attended stream. Decoder-only designs provide a simple scalable training and inference setup for autoregressive language modeling. The architectures serve different workloads, and neither is universally superior.
questions.figure:
06 · Architecture comparison

The original decoder reads encoder memory; GPT-style decoders use one stream

Both decoder types use causal self-attention on output positions. Only the original encoder–decoder architecture adds a separate encoder cross-attention sublayer.

questions.stem: How can Transformer Decoder inference be optimized for real-world LLM deployment using KV Caching, Multi-Query Attention (MQA), Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), FlashAttention, and speculative decoding, and what trade-offs do these techniques introduce in memory usage, inference latency, throughput, and generation quality?
options: KV caching stores only output logits, while FlashAttention removes mathematical attention operations and changes the model's final token predictions.
MQA stores more Key-Value heads than Query heads, and GQA prevents KV sharing, which would increase rather than reduce cache requirements.
Speculative decoding accepts all proposed draft tokens without checking a target model, so an incorrect draft automatically becomes the final output.

KV caching reuses earlier Keys and Values, MQA and GQA reduce cache memory, and FlashAttention improves attention efficiency. Speculative decoding can propose tokens more quickly while preserving a target model's distribution when correctly implemented, trading extra work for lower latency.
questions.explanation: Explanation: KV caching reuses earlier Keys and Values, MQA and GQA reduce cache memory, and FlashAttention improves attention efficiency. Speculative decoding can propose tokens more quickly while preserving a target model's distribution when correctly implemented, trading extra work for lower latency. Imagine serving an LLM to thousands of people drafting travel notes. Recomputing the entire history for each new token would waste time. A KV cache reuses past Keys and Values; MQA and GQA share KV heads to reduce storage. FlashAttention lowers memory traffic during attention, while speculative decoding lets a faster draft model propose tokens for target-model verification.
questions.technicalExplanation: Detailed explanation: KV caching saves earlier projected Keys and Values during autoregressive decoding; the model still computes new attention scores against those cached positions, so context length still costs time and memory. MQA uses one shared KV head and GQA uses fewer KV heads than Query heads, reducing cache bandwidth and memory; aggressive sharing can affect quality. FlashAttention computes exact attention using tiling and memory-efficient GPU kernels to reduce large intermediate buffers and off-chip data movement; speed depends on hardware and workload and benefits may differ between prefill and decode. Speculative decoding asks a fast draft model to propose several tokens, then a target model verifies them. Exact rejection-based verification can preserve the target's output distribution; naive acceptance or approximate verification can change results. Total gains depend on draft acceptance, batching, latency, throughput, and added verification cost.
questions.figure:
07 · Efficient inference

Caching, shared KV heads, tiling and verified drafts improve efficiency differently

KV memory still grows with context. Exact FlashAttention reduces memory traffic; properly verified speculation can preserve the target distribution, but adds draft and verification work.
